title: Bayonet Charge

cards.story: A soldier suddenly finds himself running across a field towards an enemy hedge, under fire. For a moment he almost stops and wonders why he is there. A wounded hare jolts him, and he charges on in pure terror.
cards.message: In real battle, big ideas like king, honour and patriotism disappear. All that is left is one frightened man trying to survive.
cards.why: Hughes's father fought as a frontline soldier in the First World War, and Hughes drew on those experiences for some of his finest war poems. Ted Hughes Society

title_note.heading: The title
title_note.text: A bayonet is a blade fixed to the end of a rifle. A bayonet charge is an attack where soldiers run at the enemy with these blades fixed, ready to fight hand to hand. The title sounds like a heroic action from a war story. The poem does the opposite: it shows the charge from inside one man's panicking head. The soldier is never named, so he could be any soldier. our reading

synopsis.setup: One unnamed soldier (“he”) is told about in the third person. The poem starts in the middle of the action: there is no build-up and no explanation of which war or which battle.

steps.text: “Suddenly” he wakes up to find he is already running. He is “raw”: inexperienced and hurting. His rough, hot uniform rubs his skin and he is sweating heavily.
He stumbles across a ploughed field of lumpy earth (“clods”) towards a green hedge. The hedge flashes with enemy rifle fire, and bullets rip through the air around him.
He drags his rifle along; it feels as dead and useless as a smashed arm. The “patriotic tear” he once felt for his country has turned into hot, painful sweat pouring from his chest.
Confused, he almost stops. He asks himself what huge, cold machine of fate and governments (“the stars and the nations”) has put him here, at this exact second.
He keeps running, like a man who jumps up in the dark without knowing why. Time seems to freeze: his foot hangs in mid-air like a statue.
The bullet-torn furrows throw up a yellow hare. It rolls like a flame and crawls in circles, its mouth open but silent, its eyes bulging. It is dying in agony.
He plunges past the hare with his bayonet towards the hedge. King, honour and human dignity are dropped like unneeded luxuries. Only terror drives him now, ready to explode like dynamite.

synopsis.turn: The turning point (line 9): “he almost stopped –” The rush of stanza 1 halts. For a few lines the soldier thinks instead of acts, and time seems to stand still. Then the hare breaks the spell and the charge starts again.
synopsis.ending: How it ends: not with a victory or a death, but with the soldier still charging, driven only by “His terror’s touchy dynamite.” We never find out what happens to him.
synopsis.tone: The tone: urgent, confused and frightened. There is no glory and no cheering. The only patriotic feeling in the poem is a tear that turns to sweat.

poem_intro: This poem is still in copyright, so only short key phrases are shown here. Read the full poem in your anthology alongside this guide. Highlighted words are the ones worth quoting in the exam.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>Suddenly he awoke and was running</mark> … <mark>raw-seamed hot khaki,</mark>
poem_blocks.note: We are dropped straight into the action (in media res: “in the middle of things”). He “awoke”: perhaps he was asleep, or perhaps he has only now woken up to what war really is. “Raw” is repeated: he is new and unready, and his thick uniform is rubbing his skin raw.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>Stumbling across a field of clods</mark> … <mark>Bullets smacking the belly out of the air</mark>
poem_blocks.note: He stumbles over lumps of ploughed earth towards a green hedge, which flashes with rifle fire. The bullets hit the air so hard it is as if they punch the stomach (“belly”) out of it, as if the air itself is being hurt.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>He lugged a rifle numb as a smashed arm;</mark> … <mark>Sweating like molten iron</mark>
poem_blocks.note: He “lugged” (dragged heavily) his rifle. The simile makes the rifle feel like a dead part of his own body. The “patriotic tear” he had felt for his country has become sweat “like molten iron” from his chest: the heart, where patriotism is supposed to live.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>he almost stopped –</mark> … <mark>cold clockwork of the stars and the nations</mark>
poem_blocks.note: In confusion he nearly stops. He wonders what huge machine has put him here. “Clockwork” makes him a tiny moving part, like a clock hand pointing at one second. Fate (“the stars”) and governments (“the nations”) control him.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>Listening between his footfalls for the reason</mark> … <mark>his foot hung like / Statuary in mid-stride.</mark>
poem_blocks.note: He runs like someone who has jumped up in the dark, trying to hear a reason for running. Then time freezes: his foot hangs in the air like a statue (“statuary”). The poem slows right down, just as his mind does.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>shot-slashed furrows</mark> … <mark>a yellow hare that rolled like a flame</mark>
poem_blocks.note: Furrows are lines ploughed in a field for crops; here they are “shot-slashed”, torn up by bullets. A hare is thrown up, rolling “like a flame”, crawling in circles with its mouth open in a silent scream. An innocent animal suffers because of the war.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>King, honour, human dignity, etcetera</mark> … <mark>His terror’s touchy dynamite.</mark>
poem_blocks.note: He plunges on with his bayonet. The big ideas he fought for are “Dropped like luxuries”: things you can live without. “Etcetera” dismisses them. The poem ends on terror, which is “touchy dynamite”: unstable and ready to explode.

quotes.q: Suddenly he awoke and was running – raw
quotes.means: he is in the battle before he knows it, and he is new and unprotected.
quotes.why: AQA's 2022 report says “in media res” and “suddenly” were “productive avenues” for students. “Raw” suggests he is inexperienced, and raw like an open wound.
quotes.tech: in media res opening; adverb; repetition of “raw”

quotes.q: He lugged a rifle numb as a smashed arm;
quotes.means: his rifle feels heavy, lifeless and part of his injured body.
quotes.why: AQA's 2022 report praised readings where the rifle is “so much a part of him that it had replaced his arm”: the man is becoming a weapon.

quotes.q: The patriotic tear that had brimmed in his eye
quotes.means: the love of his country that once moved him to tears.
quotes.why: it is in the past tense (“had brimmed”): his patriotism belongs to before the battle. In line 8 it becomes painful sweat “from the centre of his chest”.

quotes.q: In what cold clockwork of the stars and the nations
quotes.means: what huge, uncaring machine of fate and governments has put him here?
quotes.why: he is a tiny, powerless part of a vast system. AQA's 2022 report says strong answers saw him “becoming a robotic, unthinking weapon of war”.

quotes.q: Threw up a yellow hare that rolled like a flame
quotes.means: a hare is thrown out of the torn field, writhing in pain.
quotes.why: the hare suffers as he does: war hurts nature and the innocent too. Its silent, wide-open mouth may mirror his own terror.
the list ends on “etcetera”, as if the ideals are not worth finishing. In line 21 they are dropped “like luxuries”: in battle, they are useless.
quotes.tech: list; bathos (a grand list that ends on something flat)

quotes.means: his fear is unstable and ready to explode.
quotes.why: the poem ends on terror, not glory. He is no longer a person with beliefs, but a bundle of fear that could go off at any moment.

form.heading: The form: one moment, three stanzas, no regular pattern
explain: Third person: the poem is told about “he”, not by “I”. One AQA mark scheme (2020) calls it “first person”; that is a slip. Check the text: it is always “he”. AQA anthology (our check)
Narrative: it tells a story, but only a few seconds of one. It starts in the middle of the action (in media res) and ends before we know what happens to him.
No regular rhyme or metre: the lines are different lengths and there is no fixed rhyme scheme. AQA's 2022 report warns that pointing out a rhyme scheme “is best avoided”. AQA 2022 examiners' report
this_poem: Fast, slow, fast: stanza 1 (lines 1–8) is one long rush of action, linked by dashes and run-on lines. Stanza 2 (lines 9–15) slows down as he thinks: “he almost stopped –”. Stanza 3 (lines 16–23) snaps back into action with the hare. The shape of the poem follows the shape of the charge. our reading
Time freezes in the middle: stanza 2 ends with his foot hanging “like / Statuary in mid-stride.” The line break leaves his foot hanging in the air too.

No hero, no name: using “he” and never a name makes him an everyman: an ordinary man who could be anyone. AQA's 2022 report praised answers comparing Hughes's “anonymous individual soldier” with Tennyson's “six hundred”. AQA 2022 examiners' report
Why it matters: examiners want structure tied to meaning. Don't just say there is enjambment; say what it shows (his panic, his loss of control).
form.say: A sentence you could use: Hughes opens in media res with “Suddenly”, so the reader, like the soldier, is thrown into the charge without warning; the slower middle stanza, where he “almost stopped”, shows thought briefly breaking through before terror takes over again.

methods.title: Starting in the middle
methods.text: The first word, <q>“Suddenly”</q>, throws us into the charge with no build-up. We are as confused as the soldier. AQA's 2022 report says the vast majority of students began with “in media res” and “suddenly”, and these were productive for at least Level 3 AO2.
methods.def: Latin for “in the middle of things”: a story that starts partway through the action.

methods.title: Man and machine
methods.text: His rifle is <q>“numb as a smashed arm”</q>, and he is one hand on a <q>“cold clockwork”</q> clock of the stars and the nations. The soldier is becoming a part in a war machine, with no control over where it points him.
methods.def: showing a person as less than human, for example as a tool, machine or animal.

methods.title: Nature under attack
methods.text: Bullets smack <q>“the belly out of the air”</q>, the furrows are <q>“shot-slashed”</q> and the hare dies in a <q>“threshing circle”</q>. A field meant for growing food is wrecked. AQA's 2022 report says strong answers saw the difference between ploughed furrows and fields “savaged by the bullets”.
methods.def: giving human qualities to something that isn't human (the air has a “belly”).

methods.title: Ideals dropped
methods.text: The <q>“patriotic tear”</q> of the past turns into sweat, and <q>“King, honour, human dignity, etcetera”</q> are <q>“Dropped like luxuries”</q>. The word “etcetera” mocks the big words that send men to war.
methods.def: a sudden drop from something grand to something ordinary or silly, often for effect.

warn: Examiners warn: in 2022 AQA's report said “a mere observation of the techniques or even a vague comment about ‘flow’ and ‘pace’ will not achieve above Level 2 AO2 if it is not tied to meaning.” It also said paragraphs about “Hughes’ father as a soldier” were “not useful if they meant the student lost sight of the poem.” Keep context to a sentence, tied to the poem.

timeline.text: British Army swaps red tunics for khaki
Hughes's father fights at Gallipoli (one source)
First day of the Somme: 57,000 British casualties
The Hawk in the Rain, his first book, includes Bayonet Charge

items.text: Born on 17 August 1930 in Mytholmroyd, West Yorkshire. Aged seven he moved to Mexborough, where his father ran a shop.
He did national service in the RAF, as a radio mechanic in Yorkshire, then went to Pembroke College, Cambridge. He did not fight in a war himself, so he imagines the charge.

Britannica says his most typical poetry is “without sentimentality, emphasizing the cunning and savagery of animal life in harsh, sometimes disjunctive lines.” That fits the hare and the jerky, broken lines here.
He was Poet Laureate from 1984 until his death in 1998.
Bayonet Charge appeared in The Hawk in the Rain (Faber, 1957), Hughes's first book of poems.
items.src: Ted Hughes Society (Heather Clark); Britannica (book and date)

items.text: The Ted Hughes Society says several poems in that book show his “ongoing obsession with the First World War, in which his own father had fought.” It says Bayonet Charge speaks “to man's violent nature”.
Hughes “drew upon his father's experiences as a frontline soldier during the First World War to inform some of his finest war-verse”.
items.care: one source (INFLIBNET confirms his father served)

items.text: One university text says his father fought at Gallipoli in April 1915, was one of seventeen survivors in his battalion, was seriously wounded, and told the family stories of the fighting.
So the poem was written about 40 years after the First World War, by a man who heard about it at home. Use this in one sentence only: AQA warns against long paragraphs on Hughes's father.
A bayonet is a “short, sharp-edged, sometimes pointed weapon, designed for attachment to the muzzle of a firearm”. On the British rifle it gave “a one-metre reach in hand-to-hand combat.”
Britannica: “The development of repeating firearms greatly reduced the combat value of the bayonet.” A charge with blades against modern rifle fire is close, desperate and old-fashioned fighting.
“Rifles were by far the most commonly used weapon of the war.” A fixed bayonet “could prove unwieldy” (awkward) in a trench, which fits the soldier who “lugged” his rifle.

On the first day of the Somme, 1 July 1916, the British Army had “57,000 casualties, the bloodiest day in its history.” The infantry “were met by a storm of machine-gun, rifle and artillery fire.” Most were “inexperienced volunteers”, like the “raw” soldier. The poem does not name the Somme, so use this only as background.
items.care: link to the poem: our reading

items.text: The army switched to khaki in 1902. The uniform was “thick wool, effective in the cold winter but stifling in the summer – not to mention itchy!” That explains <q>“raw-seamed hot khaki”</q>.

The poem never names the war. It is usually read as the First World War: the Ted Hughes Society groups it with his poems about that war, and <q>“King”</q> fits a British soldier. But khaki, rifles and bayonets were used in other wars too, so present this as a reading.
items.src: Ted Hughes Society; AQA anthology (our check)

items.text: It is in the third person (“he”). One AQA mark scheme (Nov 2020) calls it “first person”; that is a slip. Don't copy it.
items.src: AQA Nov 2020 mark scheme; AQA anthology

items.text: AQA's 2022 report: “Patriotism, violence, death, inner conflict and PTSD amongst others were appropriate considerations for AO3”.
AQA's 2017 mark scheme suggests AO3 points on “the realisation of the horror / reality of war” and “the relationship between the individual soldiers and those for whom they fought”.

context.ao3: Putting it into an answer (AO3): Hughes, writing in 1957, grew up hearing about his father's First World War service, and the poem strips away the patriotic ideas that sent young men to war. By the end, <q>“King, honour, human dignity, etcetera”</q> are dropped, showing the reality of war is terror, not glory.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: 2017, 2024 and 2025 mark schemes; June 2022 report (“worked well”)
similar: Both show soldiers under fire in a hostile natural world: <q>“Bullets smacking the belly out of the air”</q> and <q>“Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence.”</q>
Both soldiers question why they are there: <q>“Was he the hand pointing that second?”</q> and <q>“What are we doing here?”</q>
Both doubt the big ideas behind the war: <q>“King, honour, human dignity, etcetera”</q> and <q>“For love of God seems dying.”</q>
different: Action or waiting: Hughes's soldier is charging in a few frantic seconds (“He was running”). Owen's men wait for days and the refrain is “But nothing happens.”
One or many: Hughes follows one unnamed “he”. Owen speaks for a group (“we”): “Wearied we keep awake”.

Nature's role: in Exposure nature is the enemy that kills. In Bayonet Charge nature is a victim: the “shot-slashed furrows” and the dying hare. AQA's 2022 report said students were “less confident” with this side of the link, so make it carefully.

comparisons.partner: The Charge of the Light Brigade
comparisons.aqa: AQA: June 2017 mark scheme; June 2022 report (Hughes's “anonymous individual soldier” vs Tennyson's “six hundred”)
similar: Both show soldiers charging straight into gunfire: <q>“dazzled with rifle fire”</q> and <q>“Storm’d at with shot and shell,”</q>
Both show men as parts of a larger machine they don't control: <q>“cold clockwork of the stars and the nations”</q> and <q>“Theirs not to reason why,”</q>
different: Honour: Tennyson ends “Honour the Light Brigade,”. Hughes drops honour “like luxuries”.
One or many: Tennyson celebrates the group, the “Noble six hundred!”. Hughes zooms in on one frightened, unnamed man.
Thinking: Tennyson's soldiers do not question orders. Hughes's soldier “almost stopped” to ask why he is there.
Sound: Tennyson's strong, regular rhythm sounds like galloping horses. Hughes's broken, uneven lines sound like stumbling.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: 2017, 2022 and 2025 mark schemes (“first-hand experience of conflict on the individual, such as ‘Bayonet Charge’, or ‘Remains’”)
similar: Both focus on one soldier and a sudden, violent moment: <q>“Suddenly he awoke and was running”</q> and <q>“all three of us open fire.”</q>
Both show the body torn by bullets with shocking images: the hare <q>“rolled like a flame”</q>; the looter is <q>“sort of inside out,”</q>
different: During or after: Bayonet Charge is a few seconds of battle. Remains is mostly about afterwards: the memory stays, “End of story, except not really.”
Person: Hughes uses third person (“he”), which keeps some distance. Armitage uses first person, in a soldier's chatty voice: “I see every round as it rips through his life”.
Fear or guilt: Hughes's soldier feels terror for himself. Armitage's soldier feels guilt for the man he killed: “his bloody life in my bloody hands.”

exam_box.question: A likely question: Compare how poets present the effects of war in ‘Bayonet Charge’ and in one other poem from ‘Power and conflict’. (AQA's exact wording in June 2017.)
exam_box.thesis: Both Hughes and Tennyson show soldiers charging into gunfire, but Tennyson presents war as a glorious group sacrifice, while Hughes shows its real effect on one man: terror that strips away every patriotic ideal.
exam_box.para: Both poets show soldiers who cannot control their fate. Tennyson's cavalry accept it: <q>“Theirs not to reason why,”</q>, and the repeated <q>“six hundred”</q> turns them into one heroic group. Hughes, by contrast, follows one unnamed soldier, who <q>“almost stopped”</q> to ask why he is in the <q>“cold clockwork of the stars and the nations”</q>. The metaphor makes him a tiny, powerless part of a machine run by governments. The effect of war is to empty him of ideals: <q>“King, honour, human dignity, etcetera”</q> are dropped, and “etcetera” mocks them. Tennyson ends by commanding us to <q>“Honour the Light Brigade,”</q>; Hughes ends with <q>“His terror’s touchy dynamite.”</q> For Tennyson, war creates heroes; for Hughes, it reduces a man to fear.
why: The thesis answers “effects of war” directly and sets up a clear difference in one sentence
Short quotations from both poems, each with a method (repetition, metaphor, the dismissive “etcetera”, endings)
Uses AQA's own 2022 point: Hughes's anonymous soldier against Tennyson's “six hundred”, and compares the two endings
